Sharks

By: Liz Fish | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
This is a story about both a great conservation success, and a massive conservation failure off the coast of South Africa.

Unique Selling Point:
We start on a high with Masa on a boat off Yserfontein with Chris and Monquie Fallows watching a superhighway of Humpback Whales. It’s a spectacular site, and one of the world’s greatest conservation success stories. ( Hopefully the boat will be surrounded by whales, but Chris has footage he is willing to share to add to whatever we capture. )
Since the international ban on whaling in 1986, whale populations have steadily increased. Chris estimates there once over 300 000 Humpback whales off our coastline, whaling reduced their numbers to 5000. Our West Coast is on a super highway of whales and the numbers keep growing. In 2019 they spotted 70, using the unique patterns on a whale’s tail fluke to distinguish them, there are now over 12,000 sightings.


Summary:
Our main character is internationally acclaimed ichthyologist and wildlife photographer and conservationist Chris Fallows - he is extremely articulate and engaging on camera.
Chris became famous in 1991 with his iconic images of “flying” sharks, and for the next 22 years he and Monique led shark cage diving trips to Seal Island (they are spectacular images to which we have full access). Shark cage diving became a booming tourist industry, South Africa was the international mecca for film crews and tourists flocking to witness these athletic creatures throwing seals into the air. It was a billion rand industry. In 2018 he took his last picture of a Great White in False Bay. The Shark Cage diving industry has all but collapsed.


Further information:
The conservation disaster- the demise of the Great White Shark. An apex creature which existed for 5 million years in False Bay, wiped out before our eyes in the last 25 years- and the Department of Environmental Affairs appears to have swept it under the carpet and moved on.
Masa will head out to Seal Island in False Bay to go shark cage diving. We see her in her wetsuit getting into the cage with the cameraman. Sadly all Masa will see are Bronze Whaler Sharks and 7 Gill Sharks, hopefully we see some damaged Bronze Whaler Sharks to illustrate the issue. Karyn Cooper owner of Apex Shark diving will talk about her distress at seeing more and more Bronze Whaler Sharks with their jaws missing or sporting massive hooks in their mouths, and speak of the need to create a no catch zone around Seal Island.
By 2014, they began noticing their numbers declining in False Bay – but this was a process that was a long time coming. In 2004 they estimated there were 1270 Great Whites, by 2012 the number was down to 900 and in 2016 Sara Andreotti research revealed the number were between 300 and 550. Chris took his final picture of a Great White in False Bay 2018.
South Africa was the first country in the world to formally protect the Great Whites. Now it looks like we are the first country to watch their demise - and do nothing about it. The reasons are hotly debated between the shark scientists, those who work for the government, and those who are independent.
Government scientists would have us believe the decline of the Great Whites has got nothing to do with humans, and that it is all down to the appearance of two Orca Killer Whales nicknamed “Port” and “Starboard”. It’s a natural phenomenon, they say, and therefore there is nothing to be done - they have just moved up the east coast.
Chris will tell us otherwise.
Independent shark scientists Sara Andreotti and Enrico Gennari have also rebutted this theory. Their research shows that it is the shark nets deployed off beaches in KZN that kill hundreds of sharks and other species every year; and the other major killer is the long line demersal shark industry, which catches and kills Great Whites, Hammerheads, Soup Fin and Smoothhound Sharks - all listed as critically endangered. Overfishing kills more than 100 million sharks a year and more than a third of shark species are threatened with extinction.
And the Department issues them licences to do so.
The story loops back to Chris – it was his pictures, drone footage and evidence that were instrumental in the conviction of the demersal long liner “White Rose” in December 2024 for fishing in a marine protected area. The judge made a landmark ruling – it was a crime against the environment (we featured this and have the footage from an earlier CB).

Chris will take Masa scuba diving in the Kelp forest in False Bay- the wonders of a marine protected area and hopefully hey wont encounter any rabid seals



Extra Budget Items:
WE need to pay R8000 for the shark cage diving . We also need to travel to Yzerfontein and be accommodated there. All the boat trips start at first light., so Masa will require 3 nights of accommodation. The shark trip and the scuba trip will happen n one day so will need and additional day for pick ups and shooting in the Simonstown museum for the whaling element.

UPS Masa
Wow! There!
Super-jackpot.
VO
Nature at its purest is both beautiful… and brutal.
UPS Chris Fallows
These two orcas, they’re probably trying to hunt this young humpback here.
VO
We’ve encountered one of its rarest events,
but it’s not immediately clear what’s happening.
UPS Chris Fallows
This is truly, truly un-flippen-believable!
Unbelievable.
VO
I’m whale watching just off the town of Yzerfontein on the Cape West Coast with conservationists, Chris and Monique Fallows.
UPS
Chris Fallows: It’s almost like they work in relay.
Monique Fallows: Ja.
VO
The excitement on board belies the panic unfolding beneath the surface.
UPS Chris Fallow
Watch out.
UPS (as hunt continues)
Chris Fallows: “It’s the old cliché “a National Geographic moment” but we’ll call it a Carte Blanche special, this one.”
VO
A young Humpback whale has been encircled by a pod of Orcas – or Killer Whales.


UPS Cris Fallows
See that orca’s probably actually biting that animal underneath right now.
VO
Orcas are highly intelligent apex predators, often working together with ruthless efficiency… just as they’re doing now. PAUSE
UPS Cris Fallows
These are the top dogs of the sea.
VO
The Humpback never stood a chance.


VO:
While it’s difficult to watch, this hunt is happening amid a great success story: Humpbacks and other whales were once exploited to near extinction. But an international ban on whale hunting in the 80’s changed that trajectory. After nearly four decades, they have returned to these waters in big numbers.
But while that’s reason to celebrate, there are warning signs that all is not well along this coast… and that’s why we’re here.
FTB
Boat on the water
on the way to dive…


UPS
Three, two, one, go! (Masa and other divers flipping off the boat)
VO
It’s not every day a city-girl gets to dive these pristine waters. This is one of many kelp forests along the Cape coast, home to an abundance of sea life.
Dive sequence unfolds


VO
Kelp is a sign of a healthy ecosystem, so it seems we’re getting something right when it comes to preserving our marine heritage. But, there’ve also been glaring failures, and one species in particular has paid a heavy price.
Archive UPS
“Tourists are anxiously waiting to spot shades under the water. Today marks 42 days since the last shark sighting. Some say a pair of Orcas have moved into the bay and are the reason the sharks have disappeared.”
VO
From about eight years ago, Great Whites began washing ashore around Gansbaai, a town in the Cape’s Overberg district, famous for shark cage diving. As many as eight carcasses were found.
Archive UPS
Dr Alison Towner: “When we cut into the shark we found that her liver was completely absent. Experts in orca research have described this sort of dexterity in other areas of the world…”
VO
Two Orcas had arrived in the area and were hunting Great Whites.
Since then, their numbers have dropped alarmingly - not only in Gansbaai but in places like False Bay, too. These days, Great White sightings are rare.
More Dive sequence


UPS OUT OF VIS



CHRIS (Around 05:30 in second cut) The loss of the GW sharks is a big, big deal. It’s like losing the lions of Africa.
VO
After the carcasses were discovered in Gansbaai, a theory blaming Orcas for the disappearance of Great Whites along this entire coast, took hold.


MASA 00:00:07:09 - 00:00:17:22 could it be just as we saw those orcas preying on that humpback whale, that that's what they did to the great white sharks as well?


CHRIS: 00:00:17:24 - 00:00:49:08 we know that orcas do predate on great white sharks in many locations in the world. But what happened in South Africa is the population decline, and crash happened long before the two notorious orcas, port and starboard, even came on the scene.




SOME UPS


VO
In some ways, the Orca theory provided useful cover, to those who have for years ignored the warnings, around a declining Great White population.


CHRIS 00:00:53:23 - 00:01:29:13 So some people like to blame the orcas because it completely absolves them from doing any management of our oceans.
VO
The numbers are alarming: 18 of 21 Great Whites tagged by a research team, off the Southern Cape since 2019 ,have simply disappeared. That’s nearly 90% of tagged sharks gone in just four years.
VO
And research shows that humans kill significantly more great white sharks a year, than orcas do.
Chris Fallows
it's such a sexy story… orcas attacking great white sharks, it's got into the public media. and that's kind of what is most people believe. But the reality is very, very different.


Transition to Simonstown


NATS and UPS
Chris and Masa chatting, boarding the vessel and heading out to sea
VO
A few days in the Cape aren’t enough to fully understand what’s led to the disappearance of an apex predator. But, this morning, I’m joining Chris on a trip that’ll help demonstrate its devastating impact.
Prepping for cage dive


VO
Chris is also a wildlife photographer who’s made a name for himself capturing iconic images of Great Whites – like these taken in 1991. He understands their plight better than most.
PAUSE
This picture is of the last Great White he ever photographed in False Bay. It was taken in 2018.


Chris
It’s hard to believe this is where some of the most famous
VO
This is one of a few shark cage diving boats operating in False Bay. But a business built on Great White sightings… has had to adapt.
Underwater cage sequence


VO
These sharks are Bronze Whalers. Still impressive up close, but lacking the aura of bigger species. They moved into the area when the Great Whites vanished.
UPS
Masa’s comment in the cage about the seal (10:25 in the 2nd cut)


KARYN 00:00:22:03 - 00:00:47:16 we used to come to Seal Island, um, and see these sharks breaching out of the water. One of the very few places in the world. And we don't see that anymore. It's gone. Um, and the sad thing is, it was on our watch.
MASA 00:00:50:12 - 00:00:53:11 when was the last time you saw a great white shark?
KARYN 00:00:55:18 - 00:01:12:12 we haven't seen a great white around the boat since March 2020. It's a long time ago.
VO
For now, the Bronze Whalers are enough to sustain Karyn Cooper’s business. But for how long? They’re already being targeted by fishing boats, and there’s little doubt, their different feeding habits, will alter this area’s delicate ecosystem.
Mood shots as boat returns to shore




This journey has been a mix of exhilaration and sadness: a celebration of our marine successes, and an acknowledgement of our failures.
Back in Simonstown




CHRIS (around 08:10 in 2nd cut) The reality is, the loss of the great white shark has simply been swept under the rug….., we have now all but lost the great white shark, the apex predator of our oceans from the South African shores and the ability for many people to generate an income, and most importantly, for us to have an intact marine ecosystem.
VO
While warming oceans have clearly impacted the Great White, our own behaviours have been even more devastating, from shark netting further along the coast in KZN, to the continued issuing of permits to meet global demand for shark meat and fins. And all this despite the Great White being declared a protected species - in 1991.







PROMO 1
Whales, sharks and orcas... and the delicate balance of our Cape marine ecosystems....
CHRIS (Around 05:30 in second cut) The loss of the GW sharks is a big, big deal. It’s like losing the lions of Africa.
As Humpbacks return to our shores in great numbers... we ask: What happened to the Great white sharks!

An apex creature which existed for 5 million years in False Bay, wiped out before our eyes in the last 25 years- and the Department of Environmental Affairs appears to have swept it under the carpet and moved on. Masa will head out to Seal Island in False Bay to go shark cage diving. We see her in her wetsuit getting into the cage with the cameraman. Sadly all Masa will see are Bronze Whaler Sharks and 7 Gill Sharks, hopefully we see some damaged Bronze Whaler Sharks to illustrate the issue. Karyn Cooper owner of Apex Shark diving will talk about her distress at seeing more and more Bronze Whaler Sharks with their jaws missing or sporting massive hooks in their mouths, and speak of the need to create a no catch zone around Seal Island. By 2014, they began noticing their numbers declining in False Bay – but this was a process that was a long time coming. In 2004 they estimated there were 1270 Great Whites, by 2012 the number was down to 900 and in 2016 Sara Andreotti research revealed the number were between 300 and 550. Chris took his final picture of a Great White in False Bay 2018. South Africa was the first country in the world to formally protect the Great Whites. Now it looks like we are the first country to watch their demise - and do nothing about it. The reasons are hotly debated between the shark scientists, those who work for the government, and those who are independent. Government scientists would have us believe the decline of the Great Whites has got nothing to do with humans, and that it is all down to the appearance of two Orca Killer Whales nicknamed “Port” and “Starboard”. It’s a natural phenomenon, they say, and therefore there is nothing to be done - they have just moved up the east coast. Chris will tell us otherwise. Independent shark scientists Sara Andreotti and Enrico Gennari have also rebutted this theory. Their research shows that it is the shark nets deployed off beaches in KZN that kill hundreds of sharks and other species every year; and the other major killer is the long line demersal shark industry, which catches and kills Great Whites, Hammerheads, Soup Fin and Smoothhound Sharks - all listed as critically endangered. Overfishing kills more than 100 million sharks a year and more than a third of shark species are threatened with extinction. And the Department issues them licences to do so. The story loops back to Chris – it was his pictures, drone footage and evidence that were instrumental in the conviction of the demersal long liner “White Rose” in December 2024 for fishing in a marine protected area. The judge made a landmark ruling – it was a crime against the environment (we featured this and have the footage from an earlier CB). Chris will take Masa scuba diving in the Kelp forest in False Bay- the wonders of a marine protected area and hopefully hey wont encounter any rabid seals
